scenario.en:
Contoso's support assistant searches **5 million** knowledge-base chunks in **Azure SQL Database** (`dbo.KbChunks(ChunkId, ArticleId, ProductLine, Embedding VECTOR(1536))`).
- Each request returns the top 5 chunks for one `ProductLine`.
- The SLA is under 200 ms per search.
- Quality must be proven: **recall@5 of at least 0.95** compared with exact search.
- Product managers also want a weekly report: for the top 100 matches of sample questions, how many come from each product line.

text.en: What is exact nearest neighbor (ENN / kNN) vector search?
Computing the distance from the query vector to every candidate vector and returning the true closest k
Navigating a graph index to return close, but not guaranteed closest, vectors
Matching identical text strings
Searching only the first k rows of the table

explanation.en: ENN is exhaustive and precise but resource-intensive. Option B describes ANN; C is exact string matching; D would return arbitrary results.

example.en: SELECT TOP (10) … ORDER BY VECTOR_DISTANCE('cosine', @qv, Embedding);

text.en: What does approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search trade, and for what?
A small amount of recall for large gains in speed and lower resource usage
Speed for perfect accuracy
Storage for compression only
Nothing; it's always exact

explanation.en: ANN uses an index to avoid scanning every vector, accepting that a few true neighbors may be missed. With recall close to 1, results are nearly identical to kNN.

example.en: DiskANN indexes power ANN in the SQL Database Engine.

text.en: According to Microsoft's general guideline, when is exact search recommended?
When the vectors to search, after predicates, number fewer than about 50,000
Only for tables with more than 10 million rows
Whenever a vector index exists
Never; ANN is always better

explanation.en: Exact search is recommended for small search spaces (≈ 50,000 or fewer vectors). The table can be larger if filters reduce the candidates. Large tables favor ANN.

example.en: A 30,000-row FAQ table can use VECTOR_DISTANCE without an index.

text.en: A multi-tenant table holds 10 million chunks, but each query filters to one tenant with about 2,000 chunks. Which approach is reasonable?
Exact search with VECTOR_DISTANCE over the tenant's rows (supported by an index on TenantId)
Always ANN, because the table is large
Full-text search only
Exact search without any filter

explanation.en: What matters is the number of candidates after predicates. 2,000 vectors is cheap to scan exactly and gives perfect recall. Scanning all 10 million isn't necessary.

example.en: WHERE TenantId = @t ORDER BY VECTOR_DISTANCE('cosine', @qv, Embedding)

text.en: In vector search, what does recall measure?
The proportion of the true (exact) nearest neighbors that the approximate search returns
How quickly the index was built
The number of dimensions recalled from storage
How often users repeat a search

explanation.en: Recall compares ANN results with an exhaustive search; 1 means no approximation loss. It isn't about build time, dimensions or user behavior.

example.en: Recall of 0.98 means 98% of true neighbors were found.

text.en: For a query, the ANN top 10 shares 9 items with the exact top 10. What's recall@10?

explanation.en: Recall@k = overlap ÷ k = 9 ÷ 10 = 0.9. Average over many queries for a stable estimate.

example.en: Report mean recall@10 across 200 sample queries.

text.en: How do you measure the recall of your vector index?
For sample queries, compare ANN results (VECTOR_SEARCH … WITH APPROXIMATE) with exact results (VECTOR_DISTANCE or VECTOR_SEARCH without APPROXIMATE) and compute the overlap
Read the recall column in sys.vector_indexes
Check CPU usage
Count rows in the table

explanation.en: Recall is relative to ground truth, which exact search provides. Catalog views don't report recall, and CPU or row counts aren't quality measures.

example.en: Store both result sets in temp tables and INTERSECT their keys.

text.en: What algorithm do SQL Database Engine vector indexes use?
DiskANN, a graph-based index that navigates to close vectors using SSD and limited memory
B-tree ordering of vector elements
Hash buckets on the first dimension
Full-text inverted indexes

explanation.en: DiskANN builds a graph to traverse quickly toward nearest neighbors, balancing memory, CPU and I/O while keeping high QPS and low latency. The others aren't vector index algorithms here.

example.en: TYPE = 'DiskANN' (the default and only option)

text.en: Which metric is the usual choice for text embeddings from models such as Azure OpenAI's?
cosine
euclidean on unnormalized vectors
manhattan
jaccard

explanation.en: Most text embedding models are optimized for cosine similarity, which compares direction rather than magnitude. Manhattan and Jaccard aren't supported metrics.

example.en: CREATE VECTOR INDEX … WITH (METRIC = 'cosine')

text.en: Your model returns unit-length vectors. A teammate asks whether to index with cosine or dot. What's true?
For unit vectors both produce the same ranking; pick one and use the same metric in the index and queries
Dot gives the opposite ranking
Cosine can't be used with unit vectors
You must create both indexes

explanation.en: When vectors are normalized, dot product equals cosine similarity, so rankings match. The important rule is that the index metric equals the query metric.

example.en: METRIC = 'dot' in both CREATE VECTOR INDEX and VECTOR_SEARCH.

text.en: When is euclidean distance more appropriate than cosine?
When vector magnitude carries meaning, for example embeddings trained for straight-line distance (often some image embeddings)
Whenever vectors are normalized
Only for full-text search
Never; it isn't supported

explanation.en: Euclidean considers both direction and magnitude; choose the metric that matches how the model was trained. It's supported for VECTOR_DISTANCE and vector indexes.

example.en: Check the model card for the recommended similarity function.

text.en: Complete the approximate top-10 search for a latest-version vector index.

questions.code:
SELECT TOP (10) [BLANK1]
       t.DocId, t.Title, r.distance
FROM [BLANK2](
        TABLE      = dbo.Docs AS t,
        COLUMN     = Embedding,
        SIMILAR_TO = @qv,
        METRIC     = 'cosine'
     ) AS r
ORDER BY [BLANK3];

text.en: WITH APPROXIMATE
WITH TIES
PERCENT
VECTOR_DISTANCE
VECTOR_SEARCH
OPENJSON
r.distance
r.distance DESC
t.Title

explanation.en: Approximate search requires TOP (N) WITH APPROXIMATE, the VECTOR_SEARCH table-valued function, and ORDER BY on the distance column ascending only.

example.en: Earlier-version indexes used TOP_N = 10 inside VECTOR_SEARCH instead (deprecated).

text.en: A query with TOP_N = 10 inside VECTOR_SEARCH fails with Msg 42274 on Azure SQL Database. Why, and how do you fix it?
The latest-version index doesn't support TOP_N; remove it and use SELECT TOP (10) WITH APPROXIMATE … ORDER BY distance
TOP_N must be at least 100
Add OPTION (MAXDOP 1)
Recreate the index as an earlier version

explanation.en: TOP_N is deprecated and only works with earlier-version indexes. The fix is the new syntax; you can't create earlier-version indexes intentionally, and MAXDOP doesn't help.

example.en: Msg 42274: Vector search with version 3 index does not support explicit TOP_N parameter.

text.en: SELECT TOP (10) WITH APPROXIMATE r.distance FROM VECTOR_SEARCH(…) AS r; returns an error. What's missing?
ORDER BY r.distance — APPROXIMATE can't be used without ORDER BY
A GROUP BY clause
A WHERE clause
OPTION (RECOMPILE)

explanation.en: Approximate queries must order by the distance column (error 42248 otherwise). GROUP BY isn't allowed directly, and WHERE or RECOMPILE are optional.

example.en: … ) AS r ORDER BY r.distance;

text.en: You want approximate results sorted by distance and then by Title for ties. ORDER BY r.distance, t.Title raises error 42271. What's the fix?
Run the approximate search in a subquery ordered by distance only, then ORDER BY distance, Title in the outer query
Use ORDER BY t.Title, r.distance
Use ORDER BY r.distance DESC, t.Title
Multi-column sorting isn't possible with vector search

explanation.en: TOP … WITH APPROXIMATE requires ORDER BY on distance ascending only. Additional sort columns go in an outer query (the documented subquery pattern).

example.en: SELECT * FROM (SELECT TOP (100) WITH APPROXIMATE … ORDER BY r.distance) AS v ORDER BY distance, Title;

text.en: Can approximate results be ordered by distance descending to find the least similar items?
No; the distance column must be ordered ascending with TOP … WITH APPROXIMATE
Yes, DESC is supported
Yes, but only with euclidean
Yes, with FORCE_ANN_ONLY

explanation.en: Approximate vector search finds nearest neighbors; descending order isn't supported (error 42271). For 'least similar' analysis, use exact queries.

example.en: SELECT TOP (10) … ORDER BY VECTOR_DISTANCE(…) DESC -- exact

text.en: A developer writes SELECT TOP (10) WITH APPROXIMATE … ORDER BY VECTOR_DISTANCE('cosine', Embedding, @qv) FROM dbo.Docs (no VECTOR_SEARCH). What happens?
It fails: WITH APPROXIMATE requires a VECTOR_SEARCH function in the query
It uses the vector index
It runs exactly and ignores APPROXIMATE
It returns random rows

explanation.en: The APPROXIMATE clause is only valid together with VECTOR_SEARCH. VECTOR_DISTANCE is always exact.

example.en: Rewrite with FROM VECTOR_SEARCH(TABLE = dbo.Docs AS t, …).

text.en: With a latest-version vector index, a query asks for TOP (5) WITH APPROXIMATE results WHERE Category = 'Technology'. Only 2% of rows are Technology. What happens?
Iterative filtering applies the predicate during the search, so it returns 5 qualifying rows if they exist
It finds the 5 nearest overall, then filters, often returning fewer than 5
It ignores the WHERE clause
It fails because filters aren't allowed

explanation.en: Latest indexes apply WHERE predicates during the search and keep searching until enough qualifying rows are found or the space is exhausted. Option B describes earlier-version post-filtering.

example.en: No need to oversample with the latest version.

text.en: On an earlier-version vector index, VECTOR_SEARCH(…, TOP_N = 10) with WHERE accepted = 1 often returns fewer than 10 rows. Why, and what was the workaround?
Earlier versions post-filter: the 10 neighbors are found first and then filtered; request more candidates (e.g., TOP_N = 50) and take TOP (10) — or upgrade the index
The WHERE clause disables the index
TOP_N is a maximum distance, not a count
The metric must be dot for filters

explanation.en: Post-filtering applies predicates after retrieval, so qualifying rows outside the first TOP_N are lost. Oversampling (or migrating to the latest index for iterative filtering) solves it.

example.en: SELECT TOP (10) … FROM VECTOR_SEARCH(…, TOP_N = 50) AS r WHERE t.accepted = 1 ORDER BY r.distance;

text.en: SELECT TOP (10) t.Id, r.distance FROM VECTOR_SEARCH(TABLE = dbo.Docs AS t, …) AS r ORDER BY r.distance — with no WITH APPROXIMATE. How does it run?
As an exact kNN search (exact nearest neighbors)
As an approximate search using the index
It fails without APPROXIMATE
It returns 10 random rows

explanation.en: TOP with ORDER BY distance but without APPROXIMATE executes as kNN. This is handy for computing ground truth with the same query shape.

example.en: Use it to measure recall against the WITH APPROXIMATE version.

text.en: What happens when VECTOR_SEARCH runs on a table with no vector index?
It still runs, performing a full kNN scan that computes distances for all rows
It fails with 'index required'
It builds an index automatically
It returns no rows

explanation.en: Without an index, VECTOR_SEARCH falls back to brute-force kNN (fine for development or small tables). Indexes are never created automatically. FORCE_ANN_ONLY would fail in this case.

example.en: Create the index once the table has ≥ 100 vectors and grows large.

text.en: When should you add WITH (FORCE_ANN_ONLY) to VECTOR_SEARCH, and what does it require?
To force the approximate index strategy over the optimizer's choice; it requires a vector index and SELECT TOP (N) WITH APPROXIMATE
To force exact search
To allow DESC ordering
To enable float16

explanation.en: The latest version lets the optimizer choose between DiskANN and kNN; the hint overrides that choice. Without an index or the APPROXIMATE syntax, the query fails.

example.en: … ) AS r WITH (FORCE_ANN_ONLY) ORDER BY r.distance;

text.en: Which three operations require the subquery pattern when combined with SELECT TOP (N) WITH APPROXIMATE? (Select 3)
GROUP BY with aggregates
Window functions such as ROW_NUMBER
UNION of two searches
INNER JOIN to another table
A WHERE predicate on the searched table

explanation.en: Aggregation, window functions, set operations, DISTINCT and extra ORDER BY columns need the search in an inner query. INNER JOIN and WHERE predicates work directly.

example.en: SELECT category, COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT TOP (100) WITH APPROXIMATE …) v GROUP BY category;

text.en: For each recent order, you want the 10 products most similar to the customer's preference vector. A CROSS APPLY VECTOR_SEARCH with an outer TOP (100) WITH APPROXIMATE fails. What works?
CROSS APPLY a subquery that contains SELECT TOP (10) WITH APPROXIMATE … ORDER BY r.distance, without APPROXIMATE in the outer query
Use OUTER APPLY with the same outer TOP WITH APPROXIMATE
Use TOP_N = 10
Per-row vector search isn't possible

explanation.en: An approximate plan can't merge many independent searches into one ordered stream; scoping TOP … WITH APPROXIMATE inside the applied subquery runs one bounded search per outer row. OUTER APPLY has the same restriction, and TOP_N is deprecated.

example.en: FROM Orders o CROSS APPLY (SELECT TOP (10) WITH APPROXIMATE p.title, r.distance FROM VECTOR_SEARCH(TABLE = Products AS p, …, SIMILAR_TO = o.pref_vector, …) AS r ORDER BY r.distance) AS vs

text.en: Embeddings are in dbo.ArticleEmbeddings; titles are in dbo.Articles. How do you return titles with approximate results?
INNER JOIN dbo.Articles to VECTOR_SEARCH(TABLE = dbo.ArticleEmbeddings AS e, …) on the article key, with TOP … WITH APPROXIMATE and ORDER BY distance
Put both tables in the TABLE argument
Create a view joining them and search the view
Joins aren't supported with vector search

explanation.en: INNER JOIN works directly with approximate search, and the TABLE alias (e) can be used in WHERE for iterative filtering. TABLE accepts one base table, and views aren't supported.

example.en: FROM dbo.Articles a INNER JOIN VECTOR_SEARCH(TABLE = dbo.ArticleEmbeddings AS e, …) AS vs ON a.id = e.article_id

text.en: In FROM VECTOR_SEARCH(TABLE = dbo.Docs AS t, …) AS r, how do you reference the Title column?
t.Title — use the alias given in the TABLE argument; r provides distance
r.Title
dbo.Docs.Title only
VECTOR_SEARCH.Title

explanation.en: Table columns must be referenced with the TABLE alias; the VECTOR_SEARCH alias can't be used for them, but it exposes the generated distance column.

example.en: SELECT t.Title, r.distance …

text.en: The searched table already has a column named distance. What happens when you reference distance in the query?
It's ambiguous, like a join between tables sharing a column name; qualify it with the correct alias
VECTOR_SEARCH renames its column to distance2
The table's column is dropped
VECTOR_SEARCH can't run on that table

explanation.en: The docs compare it to a join with a shared column name: use aliases to disambiguate, or an error is raised.

example.en: ORDER BY r.distance (not t.distance)

text.en: You want every product within cosine distance 0.3 of the query, not a fixed count. Which pattern fits?
An exact query: WHERE VECTOR_DISTANCE('cosine', @qv, Embedding) < 0.3 ORDER BY that distance
VECTOR_SEARCH with TOP_N = 0.3
SELECT TOP (0.3) WITH APPROXIMATE
A full-text RANK filter

explanation.en: Threshold queries return everything meeting a quality bar; VECTOR_DISTANCE in WHERE expresses that exactly. TOP values are counts, and RANK is a full-text score.

example.en: Tune the threshold by inspecting distances on real queries.

text.en: How should you choose a distance threshold such as 0.3 for 'similar enough'?
Test with real queries, inspect returned distances, and find where relevant results stop — it depends on the data and model
Always use 0.5 for cosine
Use the number of dimensions divided by 1,000
Thresholds aren't possible

explanation.en: Distance distributions vary by model and corpus; there's no universal cutoff. Fixed constants or formulas based on dimensions have no basis.

example.en: Plot distances of labeled relevant vs irrelevant pairs to pick a cutoff.

text.en: Order the steps to serve an approximate semantic search request.
Embed the user's text with the same external model used for stored vectors
Run SELECT TOP (N) WITH APPROXIMATE … FROM VECTOR_SEARCH(… METRIC matching the index …)
Apply filters in WHERE (iterative filtering) and join metadata tables
ORDER BY distance and return results

explanation.en: A query vector is needed first; the approximate search, filters and joins form one statement; the result is ordered by distance (a requirement of the syntax).

example.en: DECLARE @qv VECTOR(1536) = AI_GENERATE_EMBEDDINGS(@q USE MODEL m);

text.en: Why is exact search still useful in a system that uses ANN in production?
It provides ground truth for measuring recall and re-ranks small candidate sets precisely
It's faster than ANN on large tables
It's required to build the index
It isn't useful

explanation.en: ENN is the reference for evaluating ANN quality and is cheap on short lists. It isn't faster on large tables, and indexes are built by CREATE VECTOR INDEX.

example.en: Approximate top 100 → exact re-rank with another metric or business signal → top 10.

text.en: With a latest-version index, a query has a very selective filter (WHERE CustomerId = 42, ~300 rows). The plan shows a kNN scan, not the vector index. Is that a problem?
Not necessarily: the optimizer can choose kNN when it's cheaper; use FORCE_ANN_ONLY only if you have evidence the index is better
Yes, the index is corrupt
Yes, filters always disable indexes
Yes, you must drop the filter

explanation.en: Latest indexes are optimizer-driven, choosing between DiskANN and kNN based on query characteristics; scanning 300 rows exactly is fast and perfectly accurate.

example.en: Compare duration with and without WITH (FORCE_ANN_ONLY).

text.en: A FAQ table has 30,000 vectors and exact queries return in 40 ms. Do you need a vector index?
Not necessarily; exact search is recommended at this size and meets the latency target
Yes, vector search requires an index
Yes, otherwise results are approximate
No, because vector indexes need over 1 million rows

explanation.en: Below ~50,000 vectors, exact search is usually adequate and gives perfect recall. An index isn't required (exact search is exact), and the index minimum is 100 rows, not 1 million.

example.en: Revisit when the table grows or latency rises.

text.en: In EF Core 10 with SQL Server, which LINQ chain produces an approximate (ANN) vector search?
context.Docs.VectorSearch(d => d.Embedding, q, "cosine").OrderBy(r => r.Distance).Take(5).WithApproximate()
context.Docs.OrderBy(d => EF.Functions.VectorDistance("cosine", d.Embedding, q)).Take(5)
context.Docs.Where(d => d.Embedding == q)
context.Docs.FromSql("SELECT * FROM Docs")

explanation.en: WithApproximate() (after Take) adds WITH APPROXIMATE to the TOP clause of a VECTOR_SEARCH query. Option B translates to exact VECTOR_DISTANCE; vector equality isn't supported; raw SQL without vector search doesn't rank.

example.en: Map the property as SqlVector<float> with column type vector(1536).

text.en: For each statement about ANN and ENN, answer Yes or No.
ENN results are guaranteed to be the true nearest neighbors.
ANN always returns exactly the same rows as ENN.
ENN cost grows with the number of candidate vectors.
A recall of 1 means the approximate search matched exact search.

explanation.en: Exact search compares every candidate, so it's precise but scales linearly. ANN may miss some neighbors; recall 1 means no loss.

example.en: Typical production recall targets are close to 1 (for example ≥ 0.95).

text.en: Match each error or symptom to its fix.
Msg 42274 (TOP_N with version 3 index)
Msg 42248 (APPROXIMATE without ORDER BY)
Msg 42271 (extra ORDER BY column)
Warning, then slow kNN despite an index
Remove TOP_N; use SELECT TOP (N) WITH APPROXIMATE
Add ORDER BY r.distance
Move extra sorting to an outer query
Use the same METRIC as the index

explanation.en: These are the documented expected behaviors of VECTOR_SEARCH with the latest syntax and index matching rules.

example.en: SELECT * FROM (SELECT TOP (50) WITH APPROXIMATE … ORDER BY r.distance) v ORDER BY distance, title;

text.en: On Azure SQL Managed Instance with the SQL Server 2025 update policy, what's required to use vector indexes and VECTOR_SEARCH?
They're preview there; enable the PREVIEW_FEATURES database scoped configuration
Nothing; they're GA under every policy
Switch to the SQL Server 2022 update policy
They can't be used on Managed Instance

explanation.en: Vector indexes are GA in MI with the Always-up-to-date policy but preview with the SQL Server 2025 policy (and in SQL Server 2025), requiring PREVIEW_FEATURES. The SQL Server 2022 policy lacks vector features.

example.en: ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION SET PREVIEW_FEATURES = ON;

text.en: Why does ENN become impractical for very large tables?
It computes a distance for every candidate row and sorts them, so CPU and I/O grow with table size
It can't run on tables over 1 million rows
It requires float16
It returns approximate results on large tables

explanation.en: Exhaustive comparison scales linearly with data. There's no hard row limit or float16 requirement, and exact search stays exact.

example.en: 10 million × 1,536-dimension comparisons per query is expensive.

text.en: Which approach evaluates vector index type and metric choices for your workload?
Run representative queries and compare recall against exact search, latency, and resource usage for each candidate configuration
Pick the metric with the shortest name
Always choose euclidean
Use whatever metric another team used

explanation.en: Evaluation is empirical: quality (recall/relevance) and performance on your data and queries, with the metric matching the model's training.

example.en: Benchmark cosine vs dot on a 500-query sample with ENN ground truth.

text.en: Which search approach should Contoso use for live requests?
ANN: a cosine vector index on KbChunks.Embedding and SELECT TOP (5) WITH APPROXIMATE queries
ENN over all 5 million chunks for every request
Full-text search only
Random sampling of 1,000 chunks

explanation.en: Millions of vectors with a 200 ms SLA call for ANN. Exact search over 5 million vectors per request is too slow, full-text doesn't provide semantic matching, and sampling breaks relevance.

example.en: CREATE VECTOR INDEX vix_kb ON dbo.KbChunks(Embedding) WITH (METRIC = 'cosine');

text.en: How should Contoso prove recall@5 ≥ 0.95?
For a sample of real questions, compare the approximate top 5 with the exact top 5 (same filter, no APPROXIMATE), average overlap/5 across queries
Check that all queries finish under 200 ms
Count the rows in KbChunks
Read recall from Query Store

explanation.en: Recall needs ground truth from exact search with identical predicates. Latency, row counts and Query Store don't measure recall.

example.en: Exact branch: SELECT TOP (5) … FROM VECTOR_SEARCH(…) AS r WHERE c.ProductLine = @pl ORDER BY r.distance; -- no APPROXIMATE

text.en: How should Contoso apply the ProductLine filter?
WHERE c.ProductLine = @pl in the approximate query (iterative filtering), plus a B-tree index on ProductLine
Retrieve the top 5 overall, then filter in the app
Embed the product line name into the question text
Create one table per product line

explanation.en: Latest indexes apply predicates during the search, and a traditional index helps evaluate them, so each request gets 5 qualifying chunks. App-side post-filtering returns too few, embedding metadata is unreliable, and per-line tables complicate everything.

example.en: CREATE INDEX ix_kb_pl ON dbo.KbChunks(ProductLine);

text.en: How do you write the weekly report (count of top-100 matches per product line)?
Wrap SELECT TOP (100) WITH APPROXIMATE c.ProductLine, r.distance … ORDER BY r.distance in a subquery, then GROUP BY ProductLine outside
Add GROUP BY c.ProductLine directly to the approximate query
Use COUNT(*) OVER () in the approximate query
It isn't possible with vector search

explanation.en: Aggregates and window functions require the subquery pattern: run the approximate search inside, aggregate outside.

example.en: SELECT ProductLine, COUNT(*) FROM (…) AS v GROUP BY ProductLine;

text.en: Two approximate searches (for "AI" and "machine learning") should be combined into one list. How?
Put each SELECT TOP (N) WITH APPROXIMATE … ORDER BY distance in its own subquery and UNION the outer selects
UNION the two approximate queries directly
Pass two vectors to SIMILAR_TO
Average the two query vectors with + and /

explanation.en: Set operations need the subquery pattern. SIMILAR_TO takes one vector, and arithmetic operators aren't supported on vectors.

example.en: SELECT id FROM (SELECT TOP (50) WITH APPROXIMATE …) a UNION SELECT id FROM (SELECT TOP (50) WITH APPROXIMATE …) b;

text.en: You need ROW_NUMBER() over approximate results to label positions 1..100. Where does ROW_NUMBER go?
In an outer query over a subquery containing SELECT TOP (100) WITH APPROXIMATE … ORDER BY r.distance
Directly in the approximate SELECT list
Inside the VECTOR_SEARCH arguments
Window functions can't be used

explanation.en: Window functions are listed among operations requiring the subquery pattern. This is exactly how a hybrid search ranks its vector branch before RRF.

example.en: SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY distance) AS vec_rank FROM (…) AS v;

text.en: A query uses VECTOR_SEARCH without any TOP and ORDER BY t.Id. What does it do?
A full scan that computes and returns the distance for every row
An approximate top-100 search
It fails
It returns only rows with distance 0

explanation.en: Without TOP and without ordering by distance, VECTOR_SEARCH behaves as a brute-force computation of distances for all rows.

example.en: Useful for analytics on small tables; avoid on large ones.

text.en: Which statement about combining a vector index with traditional indexes is correct?
They work together: the vector index finds similar embeddings while B-tree indexes on filter columns speed up iterative filtering
A table can't have both
B-tree indexes slow vector queries
The vector index replaces the clustered index

explanation.en: The docs recommend traditional indexes on filter columns; the optimizer uses both index types. Tables can have both, and the vector index doesn't replace the clustered index.

example.en: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX ix_filters ON product_embeddings(category);

text.en: What should you do after re-embedding most of a table with a new model, given an existing vector index?
Drop and recreate the vector index so its graph reflects the new embedding distribution
Nothing; recall is unaffected
Change the metric to euclidean
Switch to ENN permanently

explanation.en: Results remain valid, but recall and ranking may degrade because the graph was built for the old distribution. Recreating restores predictable behavior.

example.en: Then re-measure recall against ENN.

text.en: Why is the small accuracy loss of ANN usually acceptable for AI applications?
Embeddings already approximate meaning, so with recall close to 1 the results are nearly identical to exact search
Users never notice any search quality
ANN is exact in practice
LLMs ignore retrieved context

explanation.en: Microsoft notes the trade-off is reasonable because embeddings are themselves approximations; high recall preserves result quality while saving resources.

example.en: Still validate recall for your data.

text.en: Which two scenarios favor ENN (exact search)? (Select 2)
Searching within one customer's 1,500 documents
Computing ground-truth results to evaluate an index
Real-time search over 20 million product vectors
A public site search with millions of articles and a 100 ms SLA
A chatbot retrieving from 8 million chunks

explanation.en: Small candidate sets and evaluation baselines suit exact search. Tens of millions of vectors with tight latency targets call for ANN.

example.en: Use both: ANN in production, ENN in evaluation jobs.
